mainTopic: Buyers of liened fields: giving up a protective תקנה, resold fields, and the seller's standing to argue against his creditor
overview: The amud continues a ברייתא in which one buyer bought all of a debtor's fields, and each claimant collects from the field that was first liened to him. The גמרא asks why the buyer cannot use his threat about the deed of the זיבורית against the נזקין claimant too. It first answers that the case involves יתומים, but then gives a new reason. The rule against collecting from sold property while free property exists was made to protect buyers, so a buyer may give it up. This matches רבא's rule that a person may refuse a תקנת חכמים made for his own benefit, like רב הונא's wife who refuses support and keeps her earnings. Next comes the case where the buyer resold some of the fields. רבא teaches אביי that a second buyer receives all the first buyer's rights, including the right to refuse that rule. רבא then rules on when ראובן's creditor may collect from לוי, the second buyer. Finally אביי rules that a seller may argue in court against his creditor who seized the sold field, and a second ruling of his begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why can't the buyer use the same threat against the damages claimant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the earlier explanation. If the buyer can push away the other claimants by threatening to return the deed of the poor field, he should be able to do the same to the person collecting נזקין.
steps.simpleTranslation: With damages too, let him say this!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the explanation it gave just before. If the buyer's threat works, it should also work against the damages claimant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the buyer could say: 'If you don't accept the field I give you, I'll return the deed of the זיבורית to the seller, and then you'll have to collect from that free poor land.' This same threat could be used against the נזקין claimant. Yet the ברייתא says he collects from the עידית, the best field.

keyTerms.meaning: Damages: the claim of someone whose property was harmed
Let him say this, meaning the same argument should apply here
The best-quality land
The poorest-quality land

phrases.english: With damages too, let him say this!
phrases.notes: 'This' is the buyer's threat from just before: 'I'll give the deed of the poor field back to the seller.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier explanation (the buyer's threat to return the deed of the זיבורית) by applying it to the damages claimant.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the buyer can force claimants onto other fields by threatening to return the deed of the זיבורית.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Consistency. If the threat works against the בעל חוב and the כתובה, it should also work against the נזקין claimant. But the ברייתא lets him collect from the עידית.

steps.title: The case is about orphans, so the threat doesn't work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets the ברייתא in a case where the debtor died and orphans inherited. Orphans do not have to pay their father's debts, so the lien rests only on the buyer. Giving the deed back to the orphans would not help him, so he cannot make this threat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what are we dealing with here? With orphans, who are not obligated to repay, so the creditor's lien rests on the buyer himself. Therefore he cannot say this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by placing the case in a specific setting: the seller died and left יתומים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יתומים are not obligated to pay their father's debts. So even if the buyer handed the deed of the זיבורית back to them, the claimants could not collect from them. The liens stay on the buyer's fields, so his threat is empty.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? The גמרא uses this to narrow the case
Orphans
People obligated to repay
A lien: the creditor's legal claim on property
Therefore

steps.confusionAlert: The claimants do not lose their claim. Because יתומים do not have to pay their father's debts, the claim cannot be pushed onto them, so it stays on the land the buyer holds.

phrases.english: Rather, with what are we dealing here?
With orphans, who are not obligated to repay,
and his lien rests upon him;
phrases.notes: Literally 'his lien lies on him.' The creditor's lien lies on the buyer, not on the orphans.

phrases.english: therefore one cannot say this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by placing the ברייתא in a case where the threat cannot work.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer could always threaten to return the deed of the זיבורית and push the damages claimant off the עידית.
steps.terutzMaskana: With orphans, returning the deed does nothing, because the claimants cannot collect from יתומים. So the threat fails, and each claimant collects from his own liened field.

steps.title: The buyer gives up the rule that was made to protect him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a different reason for the ruling. The rule 'we do not collect from sold property when free property exists' was made only to protect buyers. A buyer may say he doesn't want that protection here, and let each claimant take his originally liened field.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because the buyer says to them: What is the reason the רבנן said one is not paid from sold property where there is free property? Because of an ordinance for my benefit. I am not happy with this ordinance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new explanation of the ברייתא. The buyer may turn down a תקנה that exists only for his own benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, creditors must collect first from free property, and from sold property only from the last field sold. That rule protects buyers. Here it would send everyone to the עידית, which was bought last. So the buyer gives up that protection, and each claimant collects from the field liened to him at the start.

keyTerms.meaning: Liened property that the debtor has already sold to someone else
Free property: land still owned by the debtor, not sold
One is not paid (from that property)
An ordinance, a rule the Rabbis made
It does not suit me, I don't want it

steps.whatToRemember: A person may give up a rabbinic protection that exists only for his own benefit. Here the buyer gives up the rule meant to protect buyers, so each claimant collects from his originally liened field.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a general principle: a protective תקנה made for someone's benefit can be waived by that person.

phrases.english: Rather, it is because he says to them:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the buyer, and 'them' are the claimants.

phrases.english: What is the reason the Rabbis said
one is not paid from sold, liened property
where there is free property?
Because of an ordinance for my benefit;

phrases.aramaic: אֲנָא בְּהָא תַּקַּנְתָּא לָא נִיחָא לִי.
phrases.english: I am not satisfied with this ordinance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets aside the earlier explanations and gives a new reason for the ruling in the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reason: giving up a protective תקנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the buyer bought the עידית last, all the claimants should collect from it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The buyer waives the תקנה made for his own benefit, so each claimant takes the field originally liened to him.

steps.title: רבא's rule: you may refuse an enactment made for your benefit
steps.stepSummary: The idea from Step 3, that a buyer may give up the protection made for him, matches רבא's rule that anyone may refuse a תקנת חכמים of this kind.
steps.simpleTranslation: This follows רבא, who said: Anyone who says, "I don't want this enactment of the חכמים," when it is an enactment like this one, we listen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the answer in Step 3 rests on a known rule from רבא. A person can turn down an enactment the חכמים made for his own good.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 said the rule against collecting from sold property was made to protect buyers, so a buyer may give it up. רבא makes this a general principle: if a תקנה exists only for your benefit, you may refuse it. The words כגון זו ("such as this") show that the rule does not cover every תקנה, which leads straight into the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: In line with the view of רבא
"I don't want it." A person turns down something offered to him
An enactment made by the Sages
We listen to him. His refusal is accepted

steps.whyThisMatters: This principle shapes many cases in הלכה. A protection made for one person can be waived by that person.

phrases.english: This is like רבא's view,
phrases.notes: This backs up the answer in Step 3, that the buyer can give up the protection made for him.

phrases.english: for רבא said:
Anyone who says:
"I do not want the enactment of the Sages,"
when it is one like this,
we listen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a known source for the reasoning of Step 3.
steps.raayaObject: The claim in Step 3 that a buyer may give up the rule protecting sold property.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's rule that anyone may refuse a תקנת חכמים "such as this," meaning one made for his own benefit.

steps.title: Which kind of enactment did רבא mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבא meant by "such as this."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a clear example of the kind of enactment רבא was talking about. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא did not say that anyone may refuse any תקנה. He limited it with כגון זו, so the גמרא wants to know exactly which kind of enactment can be refused.

keyTerms.meaning: What? A question asking for a clarification
Such as this. A limit on which cases are included

phrases.english: What does "such as this" mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the limiting phrase in רבא's rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A clear example of the kind of תקנה that a person may refuse.

steps.title: רב הונא's example: a wife may give up support and keep her earnings
steps.stepSummary: "Such as this" means a case like רב הונא's. A wife may tell her husband that she will not take his support and will not give him her earnings.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like רב הונא, who said: A wife may say to her husband, "I will not be supported by you, and I will not work for you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with רב הונא's case. A wife can give up the support the חכמים gave her, and in return she keeps her own earnings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים required a husband to support his wife, and in exchange he receives her earnings. The support was made mainly for her benefit, so she may refuse it and keep what she earns. That is the model for "such as this": an enactment made for one person's benefit, which that person may give up.

keyTerms.meaning: Being supported (food and needs) by her husband
Working. Here it means giving her earnings to her husband
To her husband

steps.whatToRemember: An enactment made for someone's benefit can be refused by that person, like a wife who refuses support so she can keep her earnings. In the same way, a buyer can refuse the protection that was made for buyers.

phrases.english: It is like רב הונא's view,
for רב הונא said:
A wife is able to say to her husband:
"I will not be supported, and I will not work."
phrases.notes: She means: you won't support me, and in return you won't get my earnings. I'll keep them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 5 with a model case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "Such as this" means an enactment made for a person's own benefit, like a wife's support, which she may give up so she can keep her earnings.

steps.title: If the buyer kept only the best field, everyone collects from it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states an obvious case: if the buyer sold the medium and poor fields to someone else and kept the best one, all the claimants collect from the best field.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious: if the buyer sold the medium and poor fields and kept the best field for himself, all the claimants come and collect from the best field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new point about a limit on the buyer's ability to send each claimant to his own field. It calls this first case obvious, which sets up a harder case that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the buyer himself sold the other two fields to a new buyer, and only the best field is still in his hands. He cannot send the claimants to fields he no longer owns, so all of them collect from the best field he kept. Calling this פשיטא shows the real question is still to come.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious. Often a lead-in to the case that really is in doubt
He left over or kept
For himself, still in his possession
Let them collect

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this contradicts Step 3. The buyer may give up the protection only for fields he still owns. Here he sold the other fields himself, so he has only the best field left to give.

phrases.english: It is obvious:
if the buyer sold the medium and the poor fields,
and kept the best field for himself,
all of them come and collect from the best field;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 3 by showing a case where the buyer cannot send each claimant to his own field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the buyer sold the medium and poor fields and kept the best, all the claimants collect from the best field.

steps.title: Why everyone collects from the best field in the obvious case
steps.stepSummary: The best field is the last one, and the buyer no longer owns the medium and poor fields, so he cannot send the creditors to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the best field is the last one, and the medium and poor fields are no longer with him. If they were, he could tell the creditors: 'Collect from the medium and poor fields, because I do not want the ordinance of the רבנן.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason behind the obvious case from Step 7. The buyer no longer owns the medium and poor fields, so he has nowhere else to send the creditors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the creditors' claims fall first on the field the debtor sold last, which is the best one. The buyer's only way out would be to refuse the תקנה and send them to the other fields. Here he has already sold those fields, so that option is gone.

keyTerms.meaning: The last one: here, the field bought last from the debtor
Medium-quality land
Poor-quality land
An ordinance made by the רבנן
I am not pleased with it, meaning I don't want it

phrases.english: For it is the last one,
phrases.notes: The best field was the last one sold by the debtor, so the creditors' claims fall on it first.

phrases.english: and the medium and poor fields are not with him
so that he could say to them:
Collect from the medium and the poor fields,
for I do not want the ordinance of the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the obvious ruling stated in Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the buyer kept only the best field, all creditors collect from it, because he has no other fields to send them to by refusing the תקנה.

steps.title: What if he sold the best field and kept the others?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the reverse case: the buyer sold the best field and kept the medium and poor fields.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he sold the best field and kept the medium and poor fields, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question that flips the case from Step 7. This sets up the disagreement between אביי and רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the best field, the one the claims fall on first, belongs to a second buyer. The first buyer still owns the medium and poor fields. The question is whether the creditors must go to the second buyer's best field or may collect from the fields the first buyer kept.

keyTerms.meaning: Best-quality land
He left over, he kept
What is the law?

phrases.english: But if he sold the best field,
and kept the medium and poor fields, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל מָכַר עִידִּית, וְשִׁיֵּיר בֵּינוֹנִית וְזִיבּוּרִית, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reverses the facts of the obvious case in Steps 7-8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether creditors must collect from the best field now owned by a second buyer, or from the medium and poor fields the first buyer kept.

steps.title: אביי's first thought: everyone collects from the best field
steps.stepSummary: אביי first thinks that all the creditors still collect from the best field.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי thought to say: they all come and collect from the best field.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers a first answer: all the creditors go to the best field, even though it now belongs to a second buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His logic is that the best field was the last one sold by the debtor, so that is where the claims belong, no matter who owns it now. The words 'thought to say' signal that this view is about to be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: He thought to say: a first opinion that will be challenged
They come and collect

steps.confusionAlert: 'סבר אביי למימר' is not the final ruling. It is a first view, and רבא immediately argues against it.

phrases.english: Abaye thought to say:
They all come and collect from the best field.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: All creditors collect from the best field, since it was the last one sold.

steps.title: רבא: the second buyer gets all the first buyer's rights
steps.stepSummary: רבא argues that the first buyer sold the second buyer all his rights, including the right to refuse the תקנה and send creditors to the medium and poor fields.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: What did the first buyer sell to the second? Every right that would come to him. If the creditors had come to the first buyer, he could have made them collect from the medium and poor fields. That is true even though, when he bought those fields, the best field was still free property, and normally we don't collect from sold property while free property exists. He could tell them: 'I don't want this ordinance.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts to challenge אביי. He shows that the first buyer had the right to refuse the תקנה, and that this right passed to the second buyer. The point he is building toward continues in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A buyer acquires every right the seller had. The first buyer could have refused the protection made for buyers and sent the creditors to the medium and poor fields. So the second buyer, who stands in his place, can also refuse and send them to the fields the first buyer kept. This applies the rule from Steps 3-4 that a buyer may give up a protection made for him.

keyTerms.meaning: Every right that will come into his hand: a buyer gets all of the seller's rights
The first buyer
Free property: land the debtor still owns, not yet sold
Liened property that has been sold to buyers
We do not collect payment

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the right to refuse a תקנה made for buyers is itself a right that passes along with the land when it is sold.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
What did the first sell to the second?
Every right that will come into his hand;

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵיוָן דְּאִילּוּ אָתוּ גַּבֵּי לוֹקֵחַ רִאשׁוֹן –
phrases.english: and since, if they had come to the first buyer,
he could have had them collect
phrases.notes: Some versions have the words in round brackets; the words in square brackets are the corrected wording, and they mean the same thing.

phrases.english: from the medium and poor fields,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי דְּכִי זַבְנִי[נְהוּ לְ]בֵינוֹנִית וְזִיבּוּרִית
phrases.english: and even though when he bought the medium and poor fields
the best field was still free property,
phrases.notes: Literally 'a daughter of freedom,' meaning the debtor hadn't sold it yet. The word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and we do not collect from liened property
as long as there is free property;
he could say to them:
I do not want this ordinance;

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: מָה מָכַר רִאשׁוֹן לַשֵּׁנִי
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's view that all creditors collect from the best field held by the second buyer.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A buyer gets all of the seller's rights. The first buyer could have refused the תקנה and sent the creditors to the medium and poor fields, so the second buyer inherits that same right and can send them there.

steps.title: The second buyer inherits the first buyer's right to refuse
steps.stepSummary: רבא concludes that the second buyer, like the first, can tell the creditors to collect from the medium and poor fields, because he bought every right the first buyer had.
steps.simpleTranslation: The second buyer can also tell them: 'Go collect from the medium and poor land.' When he bought the field, he bought it together with every right the first buyer had in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his argument against אביי. The second buyer who bought the best field can also push the creditors to the medium and poor fields.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 11, רבא said the first buyer had the right to refuse the arrangement and send the creditors elsewhere. Here he adds the reason this passes to the second buyer: a buyer buys the field together with all the rights the seller had in it. So selling the best field does not leave it open to all the creditors.

keyTerms.meaning: The second buyer (he bought from the first buyer)
With the understanding that
A right or legal claim
Medium-quality land
Poor-quality land

steps.whatToRemember: A buyer steps into the shoes of the person he bought from. Every right that person had in the field passes to him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This principle explains why the second buyer is protected just like the first. רבא's next rulings build on it.

phrases.english: The second buyer too
can say to them:
phrases.notes: 'Them' means all the people coming to collect: the creditors from step 7 onward.

phrases.english: Collect from the medium and the poor land.
For when the second buyer bought,
with the understanding of every right
that the first buyer had in it, he bought.

steps.triggerLanguage: לוֹקֵחַ שֵׁנִי נָמֵי, מָצֵי אָמַר לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's argument from step 11 and overturns אביי's first thought from step 10.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: If the best field was sold, the second buyer can send the creditors to the medium and poor fields the first buyer kept.

steps.title: Reuven's creditor may collect from Shimon or from Levi
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that when ראובן sold all his fields to שמעון, and שמעון sold one field to לוי, ראובן's בעל חוב may choose to collect from either of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: ראובן sold all his fields to שמעון. Then שמעון sold one field to לוי. Now ראובן's creditor comes to collect. If he wants, he collects from this one (שמעון). If he wants, he collects from that one (לוי).
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new, related case with three people: ראובן the seller, שמעון the first buyer, and לוי the second buyer. He rules that the creditor may choose whom to collect from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ראובן owes money, and all his fields are tied to that debt. Those fields are now split between שמעון and לוי. The basic ruling is that the creditor is not forced to go to one buyer first. The next steps narrow this ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor (the lender)
If he wants, he collects from this one
One field

phrases.english: Rava said:
Reuven, who sold all his fields to Shimon,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָלַךְ שִׁמְעוֹן וּמָכַר שָׂדֶה אַחַת לְלֵוִי,
phrases.english: and Shimon went and sold one field to Levi,
and Reuven's creditor came;
if he wants, he collects from this one,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is שמעון, and in the next line 'this one' is לוי.

phrases.english: if he wants, he collects from this one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: רְאוּבֵן שֶׁמָּכַר כׇּל שְׂדוֹתָיו לְשִׁמְעוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling by רבא on the same theme of a first and second buyer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ראובן's creditor may choose to collect from שמעון or from לוי.

steps.title: Only if Levi bought medium land, not best or poor land
steps.stepSummary: רבא limits his ruling to a case where לוי bought medium land. If לוי bought עידית and זיבורית, the creditor cannot take them, because לוי chose land a creditor does not normally collect.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when לוי bought medium land. But if he bought best land and poor land, the creditor cannot collect from him. לוי can say: 'That is exactly why I was careful to buy best and poor land: it is land that is not meant for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a first limit to his ruling. The creditor can collect from לוי only if לוי bought medium land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creditor's normal collection land is medium land. לוי can argue that he bought best and poor land on purpose, to stay away from the creditor's usual land. So the creditor must go to שמעון's medium land instead.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when...
Best-quality land
I was careful (on purpose)
Not meant for you (not your proper land to collect)

steps.confusionAlert: It can seem strange that the creditor cannot take the best land. The point is that a creditor's normal collection land is medium land, and לוי picked land outside that.

phrases.english: And we only said this where he bought medium land,
but if he bought best and poor land, no,
for he can say to him:
for this reason I was careful and bought best and poor land,
land that is not fit for you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows step 13's ruling to a case where לוי bought medium land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If לוי bought best and poor land, ראובן's creditor cannot collect from him.

steps.title: Only if Levi left no similar medium land with Shimon
steps.stepSummary: רבא narrows the ruling again. Even if לוי bought medium land, the creditor may take it only if לוי left no similar medium land with שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even when לוי bought medium land, we only said this if he did not leave similar medium land with שמעון. In that case he cannot say: 'I left you a place to collect from at שמעון's.' But if he did leave similar medium land with שמעון, the creditor cannot collect from לוי. לוי can say: 'I left you a place to collect from.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a second limit. If similar medium land is still with שמעון, the creditor must collect there and leave לוי alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לוי's defense is that he left the creditor proper land to collect from. If שמעון still has medium land just as good, the creditor loses nothing by going there. Only when no such land remains may he take לוי's medium field.

keyTerms.meaning: Left over, left behind
Like it, of the same kind
I left you a place (land to collect from)

steps.whatToRemember: ראובן's creditor can take לוי's field only if both conditions hold: לוי bought medium land, and no similar medium land is left with שמעון.

phrases.english: And even if he bought medium land too,

phrases.aramaic: לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא שַׁיַּיר בֵּינוֹנִית דִּכְווֹתַיהּ,
phrases.english: we only said this where he did not leave medium land like it,
for then he cannot say to him:
I left you a place with Shimon.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל שַׁיַּיר בֵּינוֹנִית דִּכְווֹתַיהּ גַּבֵּי שִׁמְעוֹן –
phrases.english: But if he left medium land like it with Shimon,
he does not collect from him,
phrases.notes: The creditor cannot collect from לוי.

phrases.english: for he can say to him:
I left you a place to collect from.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ זְבַן בֵּינוֹנִית נָמֵי, לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows step 14 further: buying medium land is not enough if similar medium land is still with שמעון.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If similar medium land is still with שמעון, ראובן's creditor must collect from שמעון and not from לוי.

steps.title: With a guarantee, the seller may fight the creditor in court
steps.stepSummary: אביי rules that if ראובן sold a field to שמעון with אחריות, and ראובן's בעל חוב took it from שמעון, ראובן may argue the case against the creditor. The creditor cannot say ראובן has no standing, because the loss will come back to ראובן.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: ראובן sold a field to שמעון with a guarantee. Then ראובן's creditor came and took the field from שמעון. The law is that ראובן may go to court and argue against the creditor. The creditor cannot tell him, 'You are not my opponent here.' ראובן can answer: 'If you take the field from שמעון, he will come back to me to be paid.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from אביי. It says the original seller, ראובן, may stand up in court against his own creditor, even though the field now belongs to שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally only the person who owns the field can argue about it, so the creditor would like to say ראובן is out of the picture. But because ראובן sold with אחריות, he must pay שמעון back if the field is taken. That makes ראובן a real side in the case, so he has the right to argue, for example that the debt was already paid.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarantee. The seller promises to pay the buyer back if a creditor takes the field.
Seized. Used for a creditor taking a liened field away from a buyer.
Argues a case in court.
Your opponent in court, the person with legal standing to argue against you.
He comes back to me, meaning the buyer will come back to the seller to collect his loss.

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule that a person may join a court case when the outcome will cost him money, even if he does not own the property right now.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Reuven, who sold a field to Shimon with a guarantee,
and Reuven's creditor came
and seized it from Shimon,
the law is that Reuven may go
and argue the case against him;
phrases.notes: "Him" is the creditor. ראובן might claim, for example, that he already paid the debt.

phrases.english: and he cannot say to him:
You are not my opponent in court,
phrases.notes: The creditor is speaking here: 'The field isn't yours anymore, so this isn't your fight.'

phrases.english: because he can say to him:
If you take it from him, he will come back to me.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: רְאוּבֵן שֶׁמָּכַר שָׂדֶה לְשִׁמְעוֹן בְּאַחְרָיוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבא's rulings about which buyer a creditor may collect from, the גמרא moves to a related question from אביי: who may argue against the creditor in court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seller who sold with אחריות may argue in court against his creditor who seized the field from the buyer, because the buyer will come back to him for repayment.

steps.title: Second version: even without a guarantee the seller may argue
steps.stepSummary: A second version of אביי's ruling says ראובן may argue against the creditor even if he sold with no אחריות. His reason is that he does not want שמעון to hold a grudge against him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: even if ראובן sold without a guarantee, he may still argue against the creditor. He can say: 'I do not want שמעון to have a complaint against me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version (איכא דאמרי) of אביי's ruling. This version lets ראובן argue in court even when he sold with no guarantee.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without אחריות, ראובן loses no money if the field is taken, so the first version's reason does not apply. This version gives a different reason: ראובן does not want שמעון upset with him for losing a field because of ראובן's debt. Even that is enough to give him standing to argue.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say. It introduces a second version of the same teaching.
Without a guarantee. The seller does not promise to pay back the buyer.
I am not comfortable with it, I don't want it.
A complaint or grudge.

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a separate ruling. It is a second version of the same ruling of אביי, with a wider scope: it covers a sale שלא באחריות too.

phrases.english: And some say:
even if he sold without a guarantee, the same applies,
because he can say to him:
I am not comfortable
that Shimon should have a complaint against me.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁלֹּא בְּאַחְרָיוּת נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of step 16 that widens the ruling to a sale without a guarantee.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even when the sale was without אחריות, the seller may argue against the creditor, because he does not want the buyer to resent him.

steps.title: Opening another ruling: a sale without a guarantee
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins another ruling of אביי, about ראובן who sold a field to שמעון without אחריות. The ruling itself continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אביי also said: ראובן sold a field to שמעון without a guarantee...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new case from אביי. It only describes the sale here, and the ruling comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far we have only the background: a sale שלא באחריות, so ראובן does not have to pay שמעון back. That detail matters, and the next amud explains what follows from it.

keyTerms.meaning: And אביי also said. It introduces another ruling from the same אמורא.
Sold.
A field.

phrases.english: And Abaye said:

phrases.aramaic: רְאוּבֵן שֶׁמָּכַר שָׂדֶה לְשִׁמְעוֹן שֶׁלֹּא בְּאַחְרָיוּת,
phrases.english: Reuven, who sold a field to Shimon without a guarantee,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר אַבָּיֵי: רְאוּבֵן שֶׁמָּכַר שָׂדֶה לְשִׁמְעוֹן שֶׁלֹּא בְּאַחְרָיוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ruling of אביי in the same series, now about a sale שלא באחריות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only the case is set up here, a sale without אחריות. The ruling follows on the next amud.
